newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Catalans add to static in digital TV fight.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Catalans add to static in digital TV fight.

text.p: The Spanish government's Catalan allies have voiced objection to controversial new digital television regulations, a Catalan spokesman said on Wednesday.

Convergencia i Unio (CiU) has told the government a proposed digital television decree will have to be debated in parliament, with amendments being presented by opposition groups, instead of simply being voted through as initially presented.
"We'll process this (television) decree as a bill and the different parliamentary groups will present their amendments as will we," CiU's Joaquim Molins said in a radio interview.

Shortly after Spain's first digital platform was launched by CanalSatelite Digital, the government announced the decree requiring that any television decoder brought onto the market would have to be compatible with several digital platforms.
CanalSatelite's decoders do not meet the new standards, and the new norm makes it difficult for it to enter the market.
CanalSatelite comprises communications group Prisa --owner of leading newspaper El Pais--, Canal Plus, Antena 3 and several regional television channels.

The group subsequently filed a suit against Spain with the European Union Competition Commission. It said the decree favours a second digital platform, and accused the government of effectively giving more time to a competitor to enter the market.
CanalSatelite started operating at the end of January.
When announcing the new requirements for a universal decoder the government said its norms strictly complied with European Union directives.

The second platform will be operated by a group headed by domestic telephone operator Telefonica, in which the government is currently selling its last 20.9 percent stake. Its platform is not expected to be operational before the summer.

The Telefonica group includes Mexico's Televisa and the state's Radio and Television of Spain (RTVE). The head of RTVE recently resigned amid local press reports of discrepancies over the government's television policy.

A CiU spokesman said the party had not decided what their specific amendment to the regulations would be, and said they had wanted to convert the decree into a bill to prevent it from being a decision made solely by the government.
"What we wanted is simply to guarantee that every group in parliament is free to give its opinion," the spokesman said.
He reaffirmed CiU's support of the administration, crucial for the Popular Party's parliamentary majority.
"We fully back the government, especially on economic policy," he added.
Competition between the two digital platforms also centres on lucrative television football rights, which the CanalSatelite group owns.
Local media reported that a separate government proposal was aimed at opening football rights to all channels.
Catalonia's own regional TV3 has a foot in both camps, with an option to form part of the Telefonica platform, and at the same time having agreed on access to the football rights with CanalSatelite.
